steps.purpose: Use complete search and keep game rules outside the renderer
steps.context: The tactical opponent loses when playing second. Minimax passed exhaustive human replies: 82 wins and 10 draws as X; 368 wins and 153 draws as O, with no losses. The owner specified Bevy 0.20.0.
steps.thought: The opponent decision now has executable evidence. Keep Board and best_move in the engine-independent library; Bevy owns input and display. Pin Bevy exactly to 0.20.0 and check its versioned APIs before wiring the game. The browser build will run the same Rust logic.
steps.outcome: Use minimax for both marks and Bevy 0.20.0 for the interface.
steps.next_action: Build the interactive board in Bevy 0.20.0.
steps.rationale: One rule implementation serves the visual game and exhaustive checks, so the demo cannot quietly test a different game.

steps.purpose: Give the board a definite size before arranging the controls
steps.context: The first real Bevy frame showed the last row clipped and the keyboard instructions below the canvas. The canvas itself was correctly sized at 720 by 620 pixels.
steps.thought: The board used percentage width and aspect ratio inside a flex column. Its auto height did not reserve the expected space for the neighboring labels. Give both dimensions the same viewport-relative value with a 330-pixel cap, so the parent lays out the complete board and instructions.
steps.outcome: Replace the board's implicit height with matching bounded width and height.
steps.next_action: Rebuild and capture desktop and compact playthroughs, waiting for each actual input result.
steps.rationale: The board owns its square geometry. Fixing that measurement lets the parent center all the controls without offsets or hiding the clipped content.

steps.purpose: The complete board fits at desktop and compact sizes
steps.context: The viewport-unit and maximum-size combination still misplaced the desktop instructions. A definite 288-pixel board fits both supported widths. The first font also lacked the en dash used in the keyboard label.
steps.thought: Use the board's definite size and a supported ASCII range label. The real browser accepted pointer and keyboard moves; all four reviewed frames now show the complete board and instructions, with the winning row visible.
steps.outcome: Keep the definite-size board and proceed to scores and rematches.
steps.next_action: Add a match owner that records each finished round once and alternates the human mark on rematch.
steps.rationale: The fix is verified in the actual Bevy browser renderer, separately from the rules tests. The earlier visual failures remain part of the record.

steps.purpose: Keep the terminal as the stable playback surface
steps.context: The current walkthrough replaces one preformatted output or project view per action. It does not behave like a terminal session. Source snapshots and executed checks already belong to the published recording.
steps.thought: Use xterm.js as the read-only terminal renderer, rebuilding its buffer from recorded actions on seek and preserving scrollback. Build-time Shiki owns tokenization; one rendering module supplies ANSI terminal output and highlighted HTML readers. Derive unified changes only from the previous snapshot for the same file. Keep annotations outside terminal cells and expand the actual project visuals below the terminal so diagrams retain readable space.
steps.outcome: A terminal-first player, synchronized concise annotations, and a single theme/highlighting policy for the entire website.
steps.next_action: Implement the renderer and focused checks, including rapid seek, theme changes, narrow layouts, copy fidelity and earlier-record boundaries.
steps.rationale: The xterm.js API supports deterministic reset/write callbacks and resizing. Asciinema's marker navigation supports retaining the current chapter model, without pretending tool records are a captured PTY stream. No agent UI data model needs to change.
